sources.title: The Unicode Standard — Chapter 3, Conformance
sources.version: Unicode 17.0.0 core specification, chapter 3
sources.authority_reason: Normative Unicode Consortium specification, primary authority for encoding terminology.
sources.inspection_note: Directly read §3.4 D7/D9/D10/D11 and §3.9 D76–D79/D92: abstract character versus glyph/grapheme, integer code space, scalar exclusions, 8-bit UTF-8 code units and 1–4 byte UTF-8. The teaching word 字元 is user-facing rather than a claim of glyph/code-point bijection.

sources.title: Unicode Standard Annex #29 — Unicode Text Segmentation
sources.version: Revision 47, Unicode 17.0.0
sources.authority_reason: Unicode Consortium normative segmentation specification; explains why visible characters need not equal code points.
sources.inspection_note: Read §3 Grapheme Cluster Boundaries, especially “often, but not always” and multiple code-point user-perceived characters, plus no break within emoji modifier sequences. The glossary gives a simplified everyday character description, not a quantified script-frequency survey.

sources.title: RFC 3629 — UTF-8, a transformation format of ISO 10646
sources.version: RFC 3629, November 2003
sources.authority_reason: IETF standards-track original specification for interoperable UTF-8.
sources.inspection_note: Read §3 including the encoding-range table and the explicit prohibition on U+D800..U+DFFF. U+0800..U+FFFF (excluding surrogates) uses three octets; supplementary-plane Han and multi-code-point characters are not all three bytes.

sources.title: RFC 8259 — The JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) Data Interchange Format
sources.version: RFC 8259 / STD 90, December 2017
sources.authority_reason: IETF original Internet Standard for JSON syntax and parser semantics.
sources.inspection_note: Read §1 text serialization and value types, §2 JSON text, §4 curly-bracket objects and colon-separated name/value members, §9 parser transformation. JSON may be a scalar/array as well as an object; the glossary explicitly says this course commonly uses objects.

sources.title: Transparent G.1 hand calculations
sources.details:
G.1 transparent hand calculations (reviewer, not an executed calculation claim)

1. Assign f(狗)=0, f(看)=1, f(貓)=2. Reading 貓看狗 from left to right gives
   [f(貓),f(看),f(狗)]=[2,1,0]. The numbering is an explicit convention;
   it is not a learned or measured semantic ranking.
2. Eight bits each have two possible values. There are 2^8=256 bit patterns.
   As unsigned integers their minimum is 0 and maximum is 2^8-1=255.
3. A table with two rows and three entries in each row has shape [2,3].
   Axis 0 indexes the two rows; axis 1 indexes the three columns.
4. The fixed example row E[2]=[0.2,-0.1] contains two coordinates. The scalar
   index 2 is neither that row nor a learned comparison between token meanings.
   These four facts also have independent executed probes in execution-v1.json;
   this document preserves the distinction between reasoning and execution.

No empirical quality, training, runtime, memory, or token-frequency claim follows.
